oneLineAnswer: An HIV medicine that blocks a viral enzyme, used only together with other HIV drugs.
whatItIs: Nelfinavir is an antiviral medicine sold under the brand name Viracept. It belongs to a group called protease inhibitors. HIV needs an enzyme called protease to copy itself. Nelfinavir blocks that enzyme.
whatItDoes: Nelfinavir is approved to treat HIV-1 infection.
It is not a cure. The label approves it only alongside other HIV medicines.
Blocking protease stops HIV from making working copies of itself.
That lowers the amount of virus in the body.
Researchers have also tested it in cancer, including a completed phase 3 trial in cervical cancer.
howPeopleUseIt: People take it by mouth as one part of a multi-drug HIV regimen.
Labeling says it is taken with food, which raises how much drug the body absorbs.
Some trials tested ways to prevent or treat the diarrhea it causes.

commonSideEffects: Diarrhea is the most frequently reported problem, usually mild to moderate.
Nausea, rash and flatulence (gas) were also common in adults and teenagers.
In children, common problems included diarrhea, low white blood cells, rash, appetite loss and belly pain.
seriousSigns: Liver injury is rare but reported, from raised liver enzymes to acute liver injury.
New or worsening diabetes and high blood sugar have been reported with protease inhibitors.
People with hemophilia have had extra bleeding, including sudden bruising and joint bleeds.
Some people developed an inflammatory response to old, quiet infections after starting HIV treatment.
Body fat can build up or shift in unusual places during HIV treatment.
whoShouldAvoid: People with moderate or severe liver impairment should not use it.
The oral powder contains phenylalanine, which can harm people with phenylketonuria.
It should not be combined with the medicines the label lists as contraindicated.
The label advises considering other HIV drugs during pregnancy.

interactions: Nelfinavir blocks a liver enzyme called CYP3A, so some other drugs build up in the body.
Rifampin and St John's wort lower nelfinavir levels, which can let HIV become resistant.
Lovastatin and simvastatin can cause serious muscle injury when combined with it.
Triazolam and oral midazolam can cause prolonged or dangerous sedation.
Sildenafil used for pulmonary arterial hypertension is contraindicated with it.
Omeprazole lowers nelfinavir levels and may weaken the HIV response.
Hormonal contraceptives may stop working as well, so the label advises extra protection.
Quetiapine levels rise, so the label says to consider switching the HIV regimen.
It should be taken at a different time from didanosine.
pregnancyAndChildren: The label says to consider other HIV drugs during pregnancy, because liver problems were reported in pregnant patients. Registry data suggested slightly more birth defects after first-trimester exposure, but a second reference group showed no rise. The label calls that finding uncertain. In children under 2, researchers studied safety but could not establish a reliably effective dose. Safety and activity in children 2 to 13 were studied in two trials.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Whether nelfinavir helps treat cancer is unproven. A phase 3 cervical cancer trial finished, but this record holds no results.
How often serious liver injury happens is unknown, because such reports are rare and voluntary.
The pharmacokinetics of nelfinavir have not been studied in people over 65.
The label says the clinical relevance of the pregnancy registry signal is uncertain.
Nelfinavir is an older HIV drug; this record does not compare it with current options.

gaps: NCCIH has no nelfinavir page; the URL returned 404.
A LiverTox (NIDDK) monograph for nelfinavir exists, but NCBI Bookshelf blocked fetching with a bot check, so it is not cited as evidence.
The DailyMed label viewer could not be opened by direct link; only the DailyMed search results page loaded, so all label facts come from the openFDA label API instead.
No results data were captured from the completed phase 3 cervical cancer trial.
The PubChem endpoint that returns a compound description rejected the request, so the PubMed-sourced review literature was not used.
Doses are deliberately omitted from this record.
summary: This record covers what nelfinavir is, how it works against HIV, its common and serious side effects, its large drug-interaction burden, and what remains unknown, all drawn from the FDA label and PubChem.
